title: Educators’ Perceptions of Large Language Models as Tutors: Comparing Human and AI Tutors in a Blind Text-only Setting
extended_summary:
This paper asks how large language model (LLM)-based tutors compare with human tutors on key qualities of tutoring, rather than on learning gains. The authors focus on four subjective but pedagogically important dimensions: engagement, empathy, scaffolding, and conciseness. They argue that prior work has mostly compared AI tutors to no tutor or measured downstream learning outcomes, leaving open the question of how educators directly perceive the quality of human versus AI tutoring dialogue.

The study uses a blind, text-only pairwise comparison setup. Human annotators with teaching experience were asked to judge short tutor-student dialogue snippets drawn from MathDial (human tutor dialogues with simulated students) and MWPTutor (LLM-based tutor dialogues with guardrails), both centered on grade-school math word problems. Each conversation was truncated to five turns, and annotators selected which of the two dialogs was better on each metric. The paper also compares the same dialogues using three LLM judges.

The participant population consisted of 35 Prolific-hired adults with teaching experience, largely from the United Kingdom/Prolific pool, and the content domain was math word-problem tutoring. The main finding is that both humans and LLM judges generally favored the LLM tutor, MWPTutor, on all four metrics; the human differences were significant for conciseness, empathy, and scaffolding, but not engagement. The authors conclude that LLMs can already approximate or outperform human tutors on some text-only tutoring qualities, but that their perceptions are still not fully aligned with human judgments, and they note limitations related to text-only interaction, a single math domain, and reliance on simulated students.
quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed empirical comparison study with a clear methodology, but it is observational/qualitative rather than a randomized educational outcome trial. It uses blind human judgments on truncated dialogue snippets rather than direct student learning measures, so it only partially meets credibility criteria for causal evidence.
impact_tier_rationale: The study suggests potentially meaningful advantages for an LLM tutor on perceived tutoring qualities, with moderate effect evidence on several metrics (e.g. t=3.16, t=3.36, t=3.65). However, the outcomes are subjective and indirect, and the evidence does not establish impact on actual K-12 student learning or large-scale institutional outcomes.

interventions.use_case: blind text-only comparison of an LLM tutor (MWPTutor, GPT-4-based with guardrails) against human tutoring on grade-school math word-problem dialogue snippets
a guarded LLM tutoring system (MWPTutor) framed as an intelligent tutoring system with finite-state/transducer-style guardrails to generate tutor utterances
text-only tutoring dialogue interface used to present truncated tutor-student conversation snippets for blind human evaluation

finding.finding_summary: The study evaluates tutoring for grade-school math word problems using 210 dialogue pairs (n=210). Human annotators with teaching experience perceived the LLM tutor (MWPTutor) as better than the human tutor on scaffolding, with a significant advantage (t=3.16, p<0.001) and mean score 0.55; the paper also reports the LLM as better on this metric in the majority of cases.
finding.measure: Human ratings of scaffolding quality in math word-problem tutoring dialogues

finding.finding_summary: For the same set of 210 math tutoring dialogue pairs, annotators judged the LLM tutor to be more concise than the human tutor, with a significant difference (t=3.65, p<0.001) and mean score 0.55. The authors argue that the LLM more often made visible conversational progress in the truncated snippets, although raw dialogue length alone was only a weak predictor of perceived conciseness.
finding.measure: Human ratings of conciseness in math tutoring dialogues

finding.finding_summary: In 210 math tutoring dialogue pairs, human annotators rated the LLM tutor as more empathetic than the human tutor, with a significant difference (t=3.36, p<0.001) and mean score 0.65. The authors note that this judgment was noisier than other metrics, but the overall direction favored the LLM tutor.
finding.measure: Human ratings of empathy in math tutoring dialogues

finding.finding_summary: Engagement was the only metric without a statistically significant overall advantage for the LLM tutor. Across all 210 pairs, the mean score favored MWPTutor only weakly (0.25), and the reported test was not significant (t=1.32, p=0.09); the result split by scenario, with the LLM doing better when it continued from the student's solution and worse when it restarted fresh.
finding.measure: Human ratings of engagement in math tutoring dialogues

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that the LLM tutor could reduce teacher workload because it performed as well as or better than humans on several perceived tutoring qualities in 210 dialogue pairs. This is an inference about delegation and teacher burden rather than a directly measured efficiency outcome, so the evidence is indirect and qualitative.
finding.measure: Author interpretation of potential teacher workload reduction from replacing repetitive tutoring duties
